title: Stream interlock prioritization experiments
content:
Goal:
Run a compact set of heuristics and lightweight experiments that let the runtime safely overlap prefill and decode work without regressing 95th/99th token latency. We want a practical, observable policy that: preserves tail latency, maintains KV residency guarantees for streaming sessions, and increases overall GPU utilization for mixed long/short workloads.

Motivating observed mixes (from trace sampling):
- 60% short-text chat (<= 64 tokens) — latency sensitive, small KV windows
- 30% long generation (>= 512 tokens) — throughput sensitive, large KV residency
- 10% bursty batched jobs (embeddings/repurchase rerank) — tolerant, high token counts

Key constraints and invariants:
- Don’t introduce new classes of head-of-line blocking that increase 99th-token latency for short sessions.
- Keep KV residency windows bounded per-session (configurable TTL) so long-running sessions do not evict critical prefixes under overlapping policies.
- Kernel affinity: certain decode kernels are much cheaper at small batch sizes; prefill kernels benefit from wider microbatches. Avoid oscillation where we repeatedly flip kernel selection for the same slot.

Overview of the proposed runtime primitive: Stream Interlock
- A lightweight coordination layer between the prefill scheduler and decode scheduler that exposes per-stream state: phase (prefill/decoding), kv-residency, estimated remaining tokens, and a priority score.
- Interlock enforces one soft rule: at most N concurrent atomic-emit slots may be in the "decode-emitting" state per-GPU-lane, where N is tuned by SLO class. Other streams can be prefilled concurrently but are prevented from preempting decode-emitting slots beyond fairness thresholds.
- Streams have dynamic lanes: fast-lane (latency critical), fair-lane (balanced), bulk-lane (throughput). The interlock promotes/demotes streams between lanes based on recent service time and observed token emission rates.

Heuristics and signals considered for priority score:
- Remaining tokens estimate (from request metadata or model sampling).
- Observed tokens/sec for the session (short bursts vs steady long).
- Age since last emitted token (helps favor sessions that have started emitting).
- KV touch footprint (estimated prefix length) and TTL remaining.
- User-configured SLO tier.
- Historical decode kernel latency curve for the stream's model variant.

Prefill overlap policy sketches:
1) Conservative overlap (default for prod): allow prefill work to run concurrently with decode for different GPU lanes but restrict prefill to microbatch sizes capped by a function of occupied decode-emitting slots. This minimizes cross-lane interference and keeps decode kernel latencies stable.
2) Opportunistic overlap (experimental): allow prefill to run on decode lanes when decode queue depth is low and the predicted emission burst is small; prefill execution must register a grace window (e.g., 2ms) after which an in-progress prefill can be preempted for a decode emit. Preemptible prefill ops must be checkpointed cheaply (partial KV writes discarded).
3) Fusion scheduling (long-term): when a batch of prefill tasks can be coalesced with upcoming decode for the same model and device, fuse into a single fused kernel pipeline that avoids redundant memory copies and reduces cross-kernel scheduling overhead. This requires stable kernel selection and increases implementation complexity.

Microbatch elasticity rules:
- Per-stream microbatch size starts at S_min, grows by multiplicative steps while observed decode-emission latency stays below threshold and GPU utilization < U_target. On latency regressions, reduce microbatch size gradually and mark stream as conservative for a cooldown period.
- Maintain a soft global token-per-second cap per-lane to protect tail-latency tunnels.

KV cache residency and handoff rules:
- KV reservation slots are decoupled from kernel execution slots: when a prefill writes KV for a stream, it reserves a KV-residency credit for TTL_ms. The interlock will avoid demoting a stream out of fast-lane if TTL_ms remaining < demotion_threshold.
- Cohort eviction policy: group streams with similar model+prefix-size into cohorts. Evict from cohorts probabilistically under pressure to avoid pathological single-stream eviction sequences.

Instrumentation and metrics to add (minimal viable):
- per-stream lane transitions counter (promote/demote events)
- prefill-preemption count and preemption latency impact series
- kernel-affinity flips per-stream (how often we change kernels for the same session)
- decode-emitting slot occupancy histogram per-lane
- KV-residency TTL distribution and forced-eviction counts
- 95th/99th token latency delta aggregated by lane and SLO tier (baseline vs policy)

Experiment matrix (quick experiments we can run in staging):
A. Conservative overlap vs no-overlap baseline — measure 95/99 token latency and overall throughput for mixed trace replay.
B. Opportunistic overlap with 2ms preemptible grace vs 5ms — compare prefill wasted work and tail latency.
C. Microbatch elasticity ON vs static microbatch sizes — measure latency variance and GPU utilization.
D. KV-cohort eviction vs LRU — tail-latency impact on long sessions.

Success criteria (for promotion to canary):
- No more than 5% regression in 99th-token latency for fast-lane sessions compared to baseline, on representative mixed traces.
- >= 8% improvement in aggregate GPU token throughput for the replayed mixed workload (configurable target).
- Observable reduction in kernel-context-switch rate for decode-emitting slots (proxy for less jitter).

Open implementation questions and risks:
- Cost of preemptible prefill checkpointing: cheap checkpointing requires we avoid large persistent writes; measure memory overhead.
- Complexity of fused kernel path: maintenance burden vs benefit needs a perf prototype.
- Predicting remaining tokens: many clients do not send accurate lengths. Should we allow a best-effort estimator that uses early-token classifier?
- Interplay with autoscaling: lane counts per-GPU may change when autoscaler resizes; need invariants to avoid lane starvation.

Immediate next steps (2-week plan):
1) Implement interlock telemetry endpoints (slot occupancy, lane transitions, preemptions) — low-risk instrumentation PR. (owner: Evan)
2) Build a simulator that replays mixed traces and applies lane promotion heuristics offline — validate heuristics quickly. (owner: Priya)
3) Prototype conservative overlap gating (non-preemptible prefills on separate lanes) behind a feature flag in staging — run experiment A. (owner: Maris)
4) Estimate KV-checkpoint cost and implement lightweight reservation credits for TTL reasoning (owner: Tomás)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally conservative as a first step: aim for simple invariants that are easy to observe and revert.
- Focus reviews on the instrumentation choices and the success-criteria numbers — those will determine whether we can proceed to opportunistic paths.
- If you have production traces that show corner cases (e.g., many mid-length streams with oscillating token rates), please upload to the shared replay bucket and tag SRV-673.

TODOs (low-priority):
- Evaluate model-agnostic remaining-token estimators (quick LSTM classifier over first 8 tokens).
- Sketch a fallback policy that sends small decode-only fallbacks to a CPU-backed lane if GPU is saturated (costly but prevents user-visible timeouts).
- Write an ops-runbook: how to revert the interlock and drain prefilled KV safe points.

Changelog:
- 2025-09-18: initial draft
- 2025-10-03: added microbatch elasticity rules and experiment matrix
- 2026-03-02: clarified KV-residency credits and added success criteria

End of doc.
